chapter: Old New Orleans and the Twenties
title: New Orleans funeral wakes, brass bands and the Roaring Twenties
summary: Asked about the Twenties, Armstrong describes social club funerals, wakes and brass band processions in New Orleans, then says Chicago was jumping from 1918, before New York.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: You hear so much about the Roaring Twenties, I didn't live it. Could you tell me a little bit about it?

Well, I can tell you, uh, a little, a little far back than that. I'm sure you could. Well, but this is a little far back than that. I'll say first and, uh, I guess before I joined Joe Oliver, you know, I was in New Orleans during the days, uh, of, uh, dance bands, and, uh, I noticed, uh, there were such things at the club where the members would die, you know? Yeah. And the musicians that started this up in the twenties, all from New Orleans, uh, what do you call me? Yeah. So if a member died, and, uh, they lay him out in the chapel, they get what they call a wake. You know, the body's laying out in the middle of the floor, and, and the members, and, and, and a lot of church sisters would come by, they're dressing, and you sing, and, uh, you weren't a member, you get the spirit like everybody else, because, uh, we always rejoice at the day, you know, and you probably lead off for him, see? And, uh, get everybody moving, like, late at night, you wake everybody up, you feel me? And after you get them started, you go back in the kitchen, and get you a big cup of coffee, or, a little dip, whatever there, cheese crackers, you know, and so, when the next day, when they, they, they dock him up, uh, put the top of the, the bare ribs, they got a brass band there, and, uh, after ceremonies, and, uh, the wife's crying, or the relatives, and, uh, as they bring him out the door, the brass band is, uh, you know, line up. Yeah. And then, uh, bass drum, the bass drum player, hits the drum. Boom. Sleep as a boy, and you make a step and it won. Boom. Boom. Boom. Boom. Mm-hmm . And then we'd probably go into another funeral, like, and be a prayer like that, where we get to the cemetery now. We bury this land. And after the Reverend Ash, Ash, you know, whatever they say, to cover the man up, and he pulled the snare out and rolled up, and everybody, and again, we get together, they should find their places. Oh, yeah. We're taking right to where this club, remember? And that's all of it. And then we get together. They should find their places. And then... We're this club, they're the members. And that's all it is. I suppose it's hard for a lot of us to understand, those of us who didn't see it, why the singing and why the music, but actually it was a time of rejoicing in a way. Well, Johnston, they never let a man like they would in New York, sit in the chapel, for days by themselves, there's always somebody singing. And that's why when I was way back from my time, I had the chance to remember those days. And my father used to tell me, and I'll tell you about the late, the 20s, but I was in some letters. And the new people had it headlined that I was in a coma, and blah, blah, and everything like that. When I got back and saw the papers, I got scared of my friends, because I wasn't that far. And besides, they didn't have any bands over in Italy to get to play for you. Well, I mean, I wasn't going to blow, because they wasn't fair enough, though. I gave a... you want to give me a scale. You did. So when I saw the paper, coma, I said, well, when I was in New Orleans, nothing but the rich people went into coma. I thought we went into a transfer. I thought we were getting into a transfer. But you say about the ruined 20s, that's a phrase, I think. Because 1918 Chicago was jumping. 19, 19, 20, 21. That's all before that. Now, New York had to come to Chicago to get hip to what was happening. New York didn't jump till after 25, or after Jack Peaygarden and Nichols, and all them boys coming in and big. You see? But things was happening in Chicago before back in 1918.
